events.cz_name: BAYSIDE AND GULFSIDE FROM CRAIG KEY TO WEST END OF SEVEN MILE BRIDGE
events.event_narrative: A mature waterspout was reported just north of the Seven Mile Bridge.  The narrow condensation funnel cloud extended almost the entire way from cloud base to the waters surface and a spray ring was visible.  The waterspout was tilted at about a 45-degree angle midway up to the cloud base while moving eastward.  The location was estimated based on radar and satellite imagery.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A non-supercell-spawned waterspout was observed to have made landfall on the Atlantic side of Key Largo in the Silver Shores Community.  A spray ring was visible with the waterspout prior to landfall.  Photos revealed damage to a dock railing and a snapped mature coconut palm tree, but no damage to nearby homes was observed.  Based on all available information, the tornado was rated EF-0 with maximum winds of 60 to 70 mph.

events.cz_name: MONROE/UPPER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Tropical storm force winds occurred mainly in gusts across the upper Florida Keys from Islamorada through Ocean Reef.  Peak sustained winds were mainly in the 25 to 30 mph range, with peak gusts measured at 45 mph at Ocean Reef, and 40 mph at automated stations in Tavernier and Islamorada. Limited utility line damage occurred along with isolated downed tree limbs. Power outages were limited to small portions of a neighborhood or two at a time.

events.cz_name: MONROE/MIDDLE KEYS
events.event_narrative: Tropical storm force winds occurred in the middle Florida Keys from Marathon through Long Key.  Sustained winds ranged from 30 to 45 mph with peak gusts measured at 60 mph at the Florida Keys Marathon International Airport, and 58 mph at the Marathon High School as well as an automated weather station on the oceanside of Crawl Key.  Scattered tree limbs were downed, with power outages limited to small portions of a few neighborhoods at a time.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Sustained tropical storm force winds occurred in the Lower Florida Keys from Key West through the Seven Mile Bridge, and were measured in the 45 to 60 mph range.  Peak gusts of 79 mph at the Key West International Airport, 68 mph at the Naval Air Station Key West Boca Chica Field, and 75 mph at an electric substation on Big Coppitt Key. Wind damage occurred in the form of scattered large tree limbs downed, with isolated uprooted or snapped trees. Scattered fences were downed in the city of Key West, with isolated building soffit and siding damage. A few commercial business signs were blown out throughout the Lower Florida Keys.  A few gas station canopies within Key West displayed fascia damage, and one gas station canopy on Stock Island exhibited foundation failure among its four posts.  Total power outages peaked near 10,000 customers in the Lower Florida Keys, representing approximately one-third of the Keys Energy service area.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Storm surge occurred along the oceanside of the Lower Florida Keys, with a a peak storm tide from City of Key West damage assessments near 4.7 feet NAVD88 along the southwest oceanside and Truman Annex area. Values of 3.5 to 4.4 feet NAVD88 were observed along much of the oceanside of Key West and confirmed by a USGS gauge, and 3.0  NAVD88 on the southeast corner of Key West and oceanside Stock Island. A storm tide measurement of 2.8 feet was recorded by a USGS gauge on the oceanside of Little Torch Key. 93 residences in Key West were flooded with 38 classified as receiving major damage and 55 with minor damage. Numerous vehicles were flooded especially in the oceanside portions of Truman Annex, southern Bahama Village and scattered throughout the southwest and south central portions of Key West. Flagler Avenue and South Roosevelt Boulevard remained closed after the passage of Ian due to flooding and debris, with the latter buried under sand to a depth of 1 to 2 feet.  6 large concrete barriers along the oceanfront of South Roosevelt Boulevard were displaced by wave action up to 30 feet.  A second surge with storm tides peaking near 2.5 feet occurred the afternoon of the 28th as Hurricane Ian moved inland the west coast of Florida.  Impacts were limited to street flooding in Key West and along the northern portions of the larger Lower Florida Keys.

events.cz_name: MONROE/MIDDLE KEYS
events.event_narrative: Oceanside storm surge flooding occurred with storm tide levels ranging from 2.0 to 2.5 feet NAVD88.  Oceanfront street flooding along with yards and several outbuildings and sheds flooded generally less than one foot deep.  A second storm surge occurred during the afternoon of the 28th, resulting in widespread street flooding along Gulf of Mexico and Florida Bayfront neighborhoods.

events.cz_name: MONROE/UPPER KEYS

Wave overwash occurred onto U.S. Highway 1 at Sea Oats Beach on Lower Matecumbe Key.

Two waterspouts began about 6 miles south of Boca Chica Key and continued forming along a cloud line extending southwest to about 28 miles southwest of Key West.  Spray rings were not visible due to obstructed views and distance from the WFO Key West webcams. The widest waterspout formed along a disruption in the cloud line where it shifted more west-southwest.  This waterspout lasted over 30 minutes with the condensation funnel cloud extending about one third from cloud base to the water surface.  Movement of the waterspouts was toward the southwest around 10 knots.

events.cz_name: HAWK CHANNEL FROM WEST END OF SEVEN MILE BRIDGE TO HALFMOON SHOAL OUT TO THE REEF
events.event_narrative: A brief, thin waterspout was observed by a trained spotter and NWS personnel west-southwest of Key West.  The waterspout was tilted at a 45-degree angle and the condensation cloud extended one-third of the way down from the cloud base to the horizon.  The waterspout moved slowly east-southeast and had a duration of about 3 minutes.  Over the following 90 minutes, six additional waterspouts were confirmed along a cloud line extending southeast to southwest of the far western Lower Keys.  A spray ring was visible with one waterspout as it passed south of Key West.  Most waterspouts were brief in duration, however one waterspout lasted for 25 minutes.  Most condensation clouds extended only a quarter of the way down from the cloud base.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Tropical Storm-force wind impacts occurred mainly with a single rain band that passed through the Lower Florida Keys during the late morning and early afternoon hours of August 29, 2023.  Tropical storm-force wind gusts produced isolated power outages in the Lower Keys generally affecting nearly 100 customers due to downed tree limbs and downed power lines.   A couple large royal poinciana trees were felled in Key West, with one damaging a vehicle.   Maximum sustained winds of 44 knots with a gust to 55 knots was measured at an electrical substation on Big Coppitt Key, with sustained winds of 39 knots with gusts to 51 knots measured by the ASOS at the Naval Air Station Key West Boca Chica Airfield.

events.cz_name: MONROE/MIDDLE KEYS
events.event_narrative: The majority of wind impacts occurred with a single rain band that passed through the Middle Florida Keys during the afternoon hours of August 29, 2023.  Tropical storm-force wind gusts produced isolated power outages due to tree limbs contacting power lines mainly affect fewer than 20 customers at a time.  Peak sustained winds were measured at 33 knots at Duck Key with maximum gusts to 39 knots at the Florida Keys Marathon International Airport.

events.cz_name: MONROE/UPPER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Brief tropical storm force wind gusts occurred over a portion of the Upper Florida Keys during the late afternoon hours of August 29, 2023.  No wind impacts were noted.  The maximum sustained winds were measured at 22 knots with gusts to 38 knots at an electrical substation in Tavernier, FL.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: The center of Hurricane Idalia passed about 165 nautical miles to the west of Key West on a northward path through the eastern Gulf of Mexico.  The combination of an approaching spring tide and strong southerly winds sustained just below tropical storm force resulted in storm tides ranging from 1.0 to 2.5 feet above MHHW along the oceanside of the extreme western Lower Florida Keys.  Moderate to heavy ocean wave overwash and street flooding within a few oceanside neighborhoods on the southwest portion of Key West occurred within a few hours of high tide on the mornings of August 29th and 30th, 2023.  The maximum water level was measured at 1.47 feet MHHW around 8:36 AM EST at the NOAA NOS tide gauge in Key West harbor.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A brief tornado initially developed over the |southeast edge of the Eden Pines subdivision, located over the|central portion of (the island of) Big Pine Key around 6:27 AM EST.|The relatively narrow tornado moved quickly north-northwest in |the general area framed by Lantana Lane, Buttonwood and Oleander|Drives. EF-0 damage was observed via the survey included vinyl|siding torn off a portion of a home, a couple downed and snapped|buttonwood trees, and a twisted fence.  Maximum winds of 75 mph were estimated in this portion of the Eden Pines subdivision.  The directional deposition|despite relatively low volume of debris strongly suggested a |tornadic circulation at the surface along a short and narrow path.  |A resident heard a distinct audible rushing sound almost |immediately before tornado passage, notable due to the lack of any|observed wind damage off the path within the residential |subdivision. The timing of the original observation of wind |damage corresponded with the passage of a supercell on a northwest |path across central Big Pine Key and into Pine Channel.

events.event_narrative: A waterspout, as continuing of an EF0 tornado that passed through the Venture Out community of Cudjoe Key, continued northeast from U.S. Highway 1, through Kemp Channel, and passing north of Niles Road Beach.  The waterspout eventually made landfall as an EF0 tornado on Big Torch Key.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A waterspout was observed by resident video of a |mature waterspout passing just to the north of the southern end of |Cudjoe Key, entering Cudjoe Bay on a northeast path. The waterspout |made landfall in a residential section along Cudjoe Bay near Spanish |Main Drive and moved through the Venture Out residential community of mixed single |family and manufactured residences. The EF0 rating is based on tree |damage including snapped hardwood branches and a healthy palm trunk |roughly 15 feet above the ground. The top portion of the tree fell |onto a manufactured residence with major wall damage and release of |numerous roofing panels deposited as far as 300 yards to the |northeast. Siding was removed from several residences. The tornado |exited the northeast portion of the community and traveled over the |western portion of Kemp Channel, before crossing U.S. Highway One |just west of the Kemp Channel Bridge. A small hardwood tree and |several large hardwood limbs were downed to the north just west of |the western bridge abutment.  Maximum winds near 85 mph were estimated at the Venture Out community with a patch width near 120 yards.  ||The continuing waterspout observed by resident video of a |mature waterspout approaching the western shore of Big Torch Key |from Niles Channel approximately 2.5 miles north of the Niles |Channel Bridge. The waterspout made landfall as a tornado north of |Osprey Lane and moved northeast, crossing Dorn Road about three |miles north of U.S. Highway 1. Numerous large hardwood branches |were broken off from area trees with a lightweight residential |amenities deposited along a narrow path about 125 yards to the |northeast. No assessment could be made further northeast due to |dense mangrove marshland as the tornado moved toward the northern |portion of Pine Channel. Maximum winds were estimated near 75 mph with a path width of about 80 yards on Big Torch Key.

The narrow path was marked by two downed buttonwood trees, broken small and medium-sized tree branches, a destroyed plastic storage shed, and three destroyed breakaway shade canopies.  No structural damage was observed.  Estimated maximum winds were 65 to 70 mph.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A remote NWS storm survey in consultation with the Village of Islamorada Emergency Manager and several residents, social media videos and photos, as well as in-situ review of realtime Florida Department of Transportation video revealed a wet microburst occurred in the upper Plantation Key area of the Indian Mounds Trail neighborhood.  Estimated wind gusts of 60 to 85 mph occurred over an area about one to one and a half miles wide by two miles long as the microburst began on the oceanside of the Old Overseas Highway.  The straight-line winds associated with the microburst crossed U.S. Highway 1 into the Indian Mounds Trail Neighborhood.  Numerous large trees and tree tops were downed in an area over 5 blocks long, with secondary damages to several vehicles and a broken window of one residence.  Lighter but sizable yard objects including furniture, trash receptacles were tossed one or more lots downwind, with one trampoline lofted into a tree.  Several of the neighborhood streets were temporarily impassible due to the size of the tree limbs.  Some minor fascia and shingle damage was also noted at a few residences.  Approximately 1,100 residents were without power as the tree limbs downed utility lines, with one tree partially blocking northbound U.S. Highway 1.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Wind Impacts in the Florida Keys of Monroe County consisted of several rain bands and gradient winds of lower tropical-storm force.  Sustained winds in the 25 to 40 mph range with frequent gusts of 45 to 55 mph were most prevalent across the far western Lower Florida Keys and the City of Key West.  Sporadic, short-duration power outages occurred with the largest outages affecting approximately 850 customers on Stock Island during the early morning of September 27th.  Several instances of large tree limbs were downed mainly in the Lower Florida Keys along with a couple trees, with resulting utility line damage.

events.cz_name: MONROE/UPPER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Storm surge flooding along the Atlantic side of Islamorada peaked at about 1.2 feet above NAVD88 at Snake Creek, resulting in the overtopping of seawalls, docks, and parking lot flooding.  Later, as Hurricane Milton crossed the Florida Peninsula, more major coastal flooding occurred along the Florida Bay shores from Islamorada through Key Largo.  Maximum water levels were observed near 3.0 feet above MHHW at Sunset Cove, and 2.5 feet NAVD88  by the National Park Service Gauge at Blackwater Sound.  Several bayside streets in Key Largo became impassible from the morning through afternoon hours of October 10th, with one residence flooded directly.

Maximum water levels were measured at 1.2 feet above MHHW in the protected Key West Harbor, but estimated at 2.0 to 2.5 feet above MHHW along the northern extends of Big Torch Key and Big Pine Key.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A waterspout with a concentrated single vortex was |observed on the oceanside moving north shortly prior to landfall in |the Truman Annex section of Key West. The subsequent tornado moved |north through a small complex of residential apartmentments. |Numerous large hardwood tree limbs and a snapped set of umbrella |tree trunks were noted, along with removed flashing and shingles |from the corners of one of of the residential structurs. A light |pole of lightweight composite spun material snapped just above its |base along the western side of the the tornado circulation. It was |this location that the maximum estimated peak wind of 95 mph was |assessed. While not specifically rated, partially-filled trash |(approximately 96 gallons) and recycling recepticles were lofted |north and northeastward, with one impact breaking the window frame |and shattering windows on one of the apartment facilities. The |tornado bended very slightly west of due north, passing near a |chapel facility snapping numerous healthy, solid-wood large limbs |from a medium-sized gumbo limbo tree, as well as snappling the |trunks of a medium-large hardwood tree of ill health and a loaded, |unharvested medium-sized coconut palm. The differing directions of |the damage path suggested the tornado likely continued as a narrow |with estimated wind speeds of 80 to 90 mph. The tornado damage path |ended in an undeveloped portion of the Truman Annex with no sign of |continuation into the Key West-Truman Annex Inner Mole waterfront.

events.event_narrative: Hurricane Rafael produced a period of tropical storm force winds primarily across the Lower Florida Keys of Monroe County.  Sustained winds of 25 to 35 mph with peak wind gusts of 40 to 55 mph occurred, downing a few small tree limbs.  No significant power outages were reported.  Peak wind gusts were measured at 39 mph with a gust to 53 mph at the Naval Air Station Key West Boca Chica Field, and 36 mph with a gust to 47 mph at Key West International Airport.

events.cz_name: MONROE/MIDDLE KEYS

Wind gusts near 40 mph occurred, with no wind damage nor power outages reported.  Peak wind gusts were measured at 41 mph at both the Florida Keys Marathon International Airport and at an automated mesonet weather station on Duck Key.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Tropical Storm Fay crossed through the Lower Florida Keys of Monroe County during the evening of August 18.  Storm total rainfall ranged from 3.35 inches at Key West International Airport to 7.05 inches at Ramrod Key.  The highest sustained wind of 33 knots (38 mph) with a peak gust of 44 knots (51 mph) was recorded at Key West International Airport. A peak gust of 47 knots (54 mph) was recorded at Cudjoe Key.  The lowest sea-level pressure was 997.1 mb was recorded at Cudjoe Key.  Coastal storm tides were 2 feet or less above sea level, equating to a storm surge less than one foot above astronomical tide levels. No fatalities or injuries were reported in the Lower Keys of Monroe County.  25,000 people, mainly visitors and nonresidents of the Florida Keys, were evacuated. Countywide Tourism losses were estimated at 8 to 10 million dollars. Damage and preparedness costs to government facilities and infrastructure totaled 2.8 million dollars, with about one million dollars due to coastal flooding damage to roads, and 200,000 dollars due to erosion.  Approximately 120,000 dollars damaged occurred due to wind. 2 tornadoes occurred in the lower Keys, with no structural damage reported.  Total damage due to the tornadoes was approximately one thousand dollars.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Hurricane Gustav passed well southwest of the Florida Keys of Monroe County during the night from August 30 to 31, 2008. Tropical storm force winds affected the Middle and Lower Florida Keys, with the highest sustained wind in the Lower Florida Keys measured at 40 knots (46 mph) at Key West International Airport, with gusts to 48 knots (55 mph).  Storm total rainfall was less than two inches at all reporting locations in the Lower Florida Keys. The lowest sea level pressure was reported to be 1004.1 mb at Key West International Airport, and 1001.2 mb at sea at Pulaski Shoal Light, located about 7 miles east-northeast of Dry Tortugas National Park.  Coastal storm tides peaked at 2.1 feet above sea level at Key West Harbor, but were estimated at 2.5 feet above sea level along the south shore of Key West.  Property damage is unknown, due to blending of Monroe County damage assessments with Hurricane Ike, which affected the Keys less than two weeks later.  One direct fatality occurred at sea 20 miles south of Dry Tortugas... approximately 80 miles west southwest of Key West.

Storm tides peaked at 1.5 feet above sea level along the south shores of the Middle Keys, which was 1.0 foot above astronomical tides. events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Hurricane Ike passed well southwest of the Florida Keys and into the Gulf of Mexico. However, Ike's large wind field produced tropical storm force winds during September 9-10, 2008.  Storm total rainfall was highest in the Monroe County Lower Keys at Key West International Airport, where 2.31 inches was recorded.  The highest sustained wind of 45 knots with gusts to 52 knots was recorded at Key West International Airport. A peak gust of 57 knots was recorded at the NWS office in Key West.  The lowest sea-level pressure of 1004.4 mb was recorded at Key West International Airport.  Coastal storm tides measured at up to 2.2 feet above sea level at Key West Harbor, equating to about 1.2 feet of storm surge. No fatalities or injuries were reported in the Lower Keys of Monroe County. Mandatory evacuations for residents and visitors were ordered from September 6 through 7, 2008. Total damage to government property in Monroe County was estimated at $13.5 million dollars.  Approximately $1.2 million damage in debris removal and erosion occurred county-wide due to storm surge flooding, with $2.6 million estimated from combined effects from wind and wind-blown rain.  Of particular note was an estimated $7 million loss to the commercial lobster fishery due to lost and relocated traps.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: Tornado touched down on Atlantic side of U.S. Highway One and moved toward the northwest. The tornado caused minor damage to facia on a business on the bayside of U.S. Highway One, then moved into a residential area. One residence with two broken windows, and another residence had an exterior wall penetrated with a 2x4 carried from over 250 yards away from a home under construction. Several trees and large limbs downed. Estimated maximum wind speed 60 to 70 mph.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A violent waterspout associated with a supercell made landfall as a tornado in Lower Matecumbe Key at Sunset Drive and moved northwest, crossing U.S. Highway One and then along Palm Drive through a residential section near Mile Marker 74 on the Overseas Highway. The tornado damage path ended on Buttonwood Lane before reaching Florida Bay. Most damage was to deck railings, screens, windows and soffits on numerous homes. A few homes displayed more significant damage, including penetration through exterior doors and walls, with one home losing 50 percent of its roof decking. The EF1 rating with estimated maximum wind speeds of 90 to 100 mph was based on roof damage to a residence along Palm Drive. Debris from sheet metal paneling and mangrove branches may have contributed to a major power outage throughout all of the Keys from Islamorada through Key West as it was carried across U.S. Highway One and a major electrical transmission line.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A weak tornado produced EF0 damage across the extreme southeast part of Key West through south Stock Island.  The tornado was first observed by a motorist just offshore South Roosevelt Boulevard before moving briefly onshore at a hotel.  Over a half dozen palm trees with some decay were snapped at the base.  Lawn furniture associated with the hotel's tiki hut north of the tornado path were blown southeast onto South Roosevelt Boulevard in the torando's wake.  The tornado tracked northeast across Cow Key Channel before moving ashore south Stock Island along 12th Avenue.  Two trees were downed onto 12th Avenue in a northeast direction.  A deck umbrella was lofted northeast from the east end of 11th Avenue onto power lines on 5th Street, bringing down the lines and causing a power outage throughout the area.  The tornado continued northeast and likely lifted or dissipated over 5th Avenue northeast of Bernstein Park.  There, a small ornamental tree was found snapped at the base and laying toward the west partially onto 5th Street.  Several trash cans placed around Bernstein park had fallen and rolled southward or southeastward.  At the tornado path northeast terminus, a television cable line was downed.  Maximum winds were estimated at 60 to 70 mph along the path from Key West through 11th Avenue in Stock Island.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: The NWS investigated a newspaper report of a tornado at Key Largo, and found the same supercell which spawned a weak tornado in the Lower Florida Keys also caused a short-lived weak tornado near Mile Marker 104 of the Overseas Highway.  The tornado produced minor damage with some outdoor furniture destroyed and ornamental palm trees downed in a parking lot at a Florida Bay-side business, and porch screens blown out at a restaurant next door.  Maximum winds estimated at 65 mph.

events.event_narrative: A waterspout accompanying a line of severe thunderstorms moved onshore the Florida Bay side of Key Largo at the Marriott Florida Bay Resort.  A tree was blown down blocking part of U.S. Highway 1 in front of the hotel.  An outdoor day spa consisting of a thatched roof and bamboo shutters and interior mirrors was destroyed. The tornado quickly dissipated over U.S. Highway 1, and was likely a non-supercell spawned waterspout.  Estimated maximum winds were near 70 mph.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A duplex residence was severely damaged when struck by a positive-polarity lightning bolt. Lightning struck the ground near an exterior Jacuzzi in a side yard, near the front corner of the structure.  The lightning strike left a hold in the ground roughly 2 feet by 2 feet by 18 inches deep.  A ground rod and wire was installed for the Jacuzzi but not attached.  The charge followed the exterior power conduit to an exterior junction box, where the box's cover was blown free.  Wires were charred, the conduit destroyed.  The residence's washer/dryer electric supply was charred.  The electric meter box exploded according to the responding fire unit, with wires charred and burned and all connections melted.  In the front of the residence, wood was charred under metal screws securing the exterior soffit.  Aluminum frames for glass jalaousie windows in the front of the residence were melted with windows knocked out.  Light bulbs in various locations throughout the residence were blown, including the bedroom lamps and ceiling fixture, bathroom wall fixture, and kitchen ceiling light fixture.  The bathroom mirror was shattered.  The residence was declared unfit for occupation due to damage to the electrical system, although no fire resulted.  Keys Energy Services replaced a blown fuse for a transformer serving the residence, and three other residences had tripped circuits but no permanent damage was reported.  The struck residence was occupied by one female at the time of the strike, who was observed by rescue personnel to not have any injuries.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: The collective effects of Tropical Storm Isaac during the period of August 24 through 27, resulted in over 2.1 million dollars in damages for the Florida Keys of Monroe County.  Within the overall total, including damages and expenditures for Tropical Storm Isaac operations, over 300,000 dollars was directly associated with coastal flooding damage within the City of Key West and approximately 130,000 dollars due to wind damage. ||The center of Tropical Storm Isaac passed approximately 40 nautical miles to the south southwest of Key West the afternoon of August 26.  ||Maximum Storm Tides in the Lower Florida Keys of Monroe County were measured at 2.92 feet above mean lower low water at Key West Harbor, with estimates up to 3.25 feet above mean lower low water on the oceanside at Key West.||The minimum pressure measured in the Lower Florida Keys of Monroe County was 997.3 mb at both Key West International Airport and the Naval Air Station Key West.||Maximum sustained winds in the Lower Florida Keys of Monroe County were measured at 41 mph at Cudjoe Key, 40 mph at the Naval Air Station Key West, and 39 mph at Key West International Airport.  Peak gusts of 54 mph were measured at the Key West International Airport and the U.S. Coast Guard Sector Key West.||Rainfall totals in the Lower Keys of Monroe County ranged from near 1.25 inches at the Naval Air Station Key West to 3.26 inches at Big Pine Key.

events.cz_name: MONROE/MIDDLE KEYS
events.event_narrative: The collective effects of Tropical Storm Isaac during the period of August 24 through 27, resulted in over 2.1 million dollars in damages for the Florida Keys of Monroe County.  Within the overall total, including damages and expenditures for Tropical Storm Isaac operations, over 200,000 dollars was directly associated with coastal flooding damage within the City of Key West and approximately 150,000 dollars due to wind damage. ||The center of Tropical Storm Isaac passed approximately 40 nautical miles to the south southwest of Key West the afternoon of August 26.  ||Maximum Storm Tides in the Middle Florida Keys of Monroe County were measured at 1.87 feet above mean lower low water at Vaca Key near the U.S. Coast Guard Station Marathon, with estimates up to 2.25 feet above mean lower low water on the oceanside at Marathon and Key Colony Beach.||The minimum pressure measured in the Middle Florida Keys of Monroe County was 1000.0 mb at an automated Citizen Weather Observing Station on Long Key.||Maximum sustained winds in the Middle Florida Keys of Monroe County were measured at 44 mph at an automated Citizen Weather Observing Station on Long Key, with peak gusts to 59 mph.||Rainfall totals in the Middle Keys of Monroe County ranged from 2.82 inches at the Marathon Florida Keys Airport to 3.83 inches at Curry Hammock State Park.

events.cz_name: MONROE/UPPER KEYS
events.event_narrative: The collective effects of Tropical Storm Isaac during the period of August 24 through 27, resulted in over 2.1 million dollars in damages for the Florida Keys of Monroe County.  Within the overall total, including damages and expenditures for Tropical Storm Isaac operations, approximately 40,000 dollars was due to wind damage. ||The center of Tropical Storm Isaac passed approximately 40 nautical miles to the south southwest of Key West the afternoon of August 26.  ||Maximum Storm Tides in the Upper Florida Keys of Monroe County were estimated near 2 feet above mean lower low water on the oceanside.||The minimum pressure measured in the Upper Florida Keys of Monroe County was 1000.2 mb on Upper Matecumbe Key. ||Maximum sustained winds in the Upper Florida Keys of Monroe County were measured at 36 mph at a Florida Department of Transportation Test Pad on Tea Table Key, with peak gusts to 54 mph at an automated Weatherflow station on Upper Matecumbe Key.||Rainfall totals in the Upper Keys of Monroe County ranged from 3.90 inches at in Key Largo to 7.94 inches on Upper Matecumbe Key.

events.cz_name: MONROE/UPPER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Hurricane Sandy produced tropical storm force wind gusts in the Upper Florida Keys as it moved north through the central and northwest Bahamas.  Maximum sustained winds ranged from 25 to 32 mph from Key Largo through Upper Matecumbe Key, with peak gusts measured at 48 mph at Upper Matecumbe and 44 mph at Key Largo.  Very minor wind damage occurred, from isolated power outages due to tree limbs contacting power lines. Approximately 700 customers were without power on October 25th.  As Hurricane Sandy continued to move north of the Bahamas, strong northwest winds across the eastern Gulf of Mexico pushed higher-than-normal tides into Florida Bay, reaching up to 2.5 feet above mean sea level and causing flooding of secondary streets.  The tides remained high due to normally higher full moon spring tide through the early part of the following week.  No flood damage was reported.

events.cz_name: MONROE/MIDDLE KEYS
events.event_narrative: Hurricane Sandy produced tropical storm force wind gusts in the Upper Florida Keys as it moved north through the central and northwest Bahamas.  Due to outer rain bands forming well outside the central circulation of Hurricane Sandy, tropical storm force wind gusts began in the Middle Florida Keys before any other portion of the island chain.  Maximum sustained winds ranged from 30 to 40 mph from Long Key through Marathon, with peak gusts measured at 58 mph at Long Key, and 47 mph at Marathon.  Very minor wind damage occurred, from isolated power outages due to tree limbs contacting power lines. Approximately 10 customers were without power on October 25th.  As Hurricane Sandy continued to move north of the Bahamas, strong northwest winds across the eastern Gulf of Mexico pushed higher-than-normal tides into Florida Bay, reaching up to 2.5 feet above mean sea level and causing flooding of docks and yards.  The tides remained high due to normally higher full moon spring tide through the early part of the following week.  No flood damage was reported.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Hurricane Sandy produced tropical storm force wind gusts in the Upper Florida Keys as it moved north through the central and northwest Bahamas.  Maximum sustained winds ranged from 25 to 40 mph from Ramrod Key through Key West, with peak gusts measured at 58 mph at Cudjoe Key and 45 mph at the Naval Air Station at Boca Chica.  No wind damage was reported.  As Hurricane Sandy continued to move north of the Bahamas, strong northwest winds across the eastern Gulf of Mexico pushed higher-than-normal tides into the nearshore waters along the Lower Keys, reaching up to 2.5 feet above mean sea level and causing flooding of secondary roads and low lying streets.  The tides remained high due to normally higher full moon spring tide through the early part of the following week.  Minor flood damage was reported.

events.cz_name: MONROE/UPPER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Storm Tide flooding began in the Upper Florida Keys as strong northwest winds around the periphery of Hurricane Sandy piled water into Florida Bay.  Tides remained high for about one week due to the approach of the full moon spring tide.  Tide levels reached up to 2.5 feet above mean sea level, causing flooding of streets along Florida Bay of 6 to 12 inches.  No damage was reported, however numerous residents in the Florida Bay communities from Mile marker 101 through 106 could not leave their homes.  Monroe County Transportation provided special shuttle service until waters receded.  No flood damage was reported.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Storm tide flooding occurred as strong northwest winds around the periphery of Hurricane Sandy piled water along the north and west shores of the Lower Florida Keys. Flooding of secondary streets and private roads of 4 to 6 inches' depth was noted along the northern end of Big Pine Key, Sugarloaf Key and Key West.  Minor damage occurred when a spa pump at ground level was flooded on Big Pine Key.  Tides gradually receded by the early morning hours of October 31st.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A waterspout was observed by the public, backlit by frequent lightning strikes approaching long beach estates from the west-southwest, passing to the south of the Newfound Harbor Keys.  The waterspout moved ashore along the oceanside of Long Beach Drive and passed over the public observer's property, a bed-and-breakfast inn.  It was at this landfall location that the tornado was at its maximum intensity and width of about 80 yards.  Widespread damage to large limbs of native hardwood trees occurred, and one royal palm snapped at a level above 15 feet.  A ground deck with four kayaks became airborne with the dock dropped within mangroves beyond 30 yards from the original location.  A large unmounted above-ground cistern containing nearly 200 gallons of water slide just over 15 yards, knocking a large camping trailer off its front mount.  Bolts securing a large grill to wood ground decking were sheared off.  While numerous tables and lounge chairs were carried to the leeward side of the property, one 40-lb steel lounge chair was lifted to the edge of the roof line of the two-story residence, crushing the rain gutter, before settling in the lee of the structure.  Small gravel and pea rock along the waterfront caused moderate to severe paint chipping on the oceanside of several homes.  Screens including their wood frames were torn off several residences' oceanside porches, with one home losing about 40 percent of its oceanside vinyl siding.  A phone line was downed along Long Beach Drive.  ||The tornado continued across mud flats along the southeast edge of Coupon Bight, where only isolated damage to mangrove branches was observed.  Small limbs were observed downed across Long Beach Drive between Southeast Point and U.S. Highway 1, eventually crossed through a campground just south of the Spanish Harbor Channel Bridge.  Several tents including one large aluminum-framed dome tent strucutre were overturned before the tornado likely passed into Spanish Harbor Channel.   The intensity of the tornado at Spanish Harbor Channel had decreased since its original landfall with estimated winds near 60 mph.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: Two lightning strikes occurred to the Bonefish Towers complex in the Coco Plum section of the city of Marathon.  The first bolt was observed to strike a small grouping of palm trees, which were set on fire.  The local fire department extinguished the fire.  A second strike to the main rooftop dryer vent melted the aluminum framing around dryer lint screens on the 4th, 7th, 8th and 9th floors along the southeast corner of the condominum tower.  Laundry rooms exist on all floors of the condominium except the 14th floor penthouse.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A police officer was injured when his motorcycle was struck, possibly indirectly, by lightning.  It was unknown whether the original lightning strike was to a utility pole or directly to the right-hand handlebar of the motorcycle.  The officer was waiting at a traffic signal at Palm Avenue and North Roosevelt Boulevard while returning to the Key West Police Station in order to switch to his assigned car after hearing thunder.  The officer experienced a significant jolt which threw his right arm backward, causing a shoulder injury.  The officer remained conscious and was able to call for rescue service using his own radio.   The officer was admitted for overnight observation and medical testing and did not receive any burns from the lightning strike.  The officer was released shortly thereafter and was expected to return to duty soon.

events.cz_name: Monroe/Upper Keys
events.event_narrative: Continuous coastal flooding of streets began approximately 17:00 EST on September  21st in the area of Adams and Shaw Drive in North Key Largo's bayside, gradually expanding to adjacent streets throughout the Blackwater Sound and Sexton Cove shorelines.  While no homes or businesses were flooded, the depth of water reached as high as 0.8 feet by September 30th, with a couple streets becoming impassable to small vehicles.  The flooding was confirmed by Monroe County Emergency Management and Key Largo Fire Rescue.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A waterspout was observed as a condensation funnel cloud over a marine basin approximately 630 am EST north of Key Colony Beach and just west of the Coco Plum Drive causeway.   The waterspout was observed crossing the causeway as a tornado at a seafood distribution business damaging a metal overhang.  Tarps and canvas coverings on vessels docked in the adjacent marina were partially or completely removed, with a few torn.   No structural damage to buildings or vessels was observed.  The tornado exited the causeway as a waterspout and dissipated very shortly thereafter.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: The examination of a video of the event and survey results revealed the first instance of damage to a hollow metal tube roof structure topped with plastic or hard vinyl |covering, affixed to wood two-by-four supports of a fishing house shed just northwest of Safe Harbor on Stock Island. The roof structure was flipped airborne and deposited about 20 to 30 feet to the west-northwest of the original location. The tornado moved just south of due west, and lifted a boat tarp including hollow tubing framework 30 to 40 feet into the air, depositing it in a stand of Australian pines over 100 feet to the northwest. A 15-by-15 foot folding tent structure topped with boat covering structure was lifted airborne for several seconds and destroyed 20 to 30 feet from its original location. Another hollow tubing boat covering frame, affixed via screws through flat plywood shims to another fish house shack, and used as a shade overhang, was removed as a single unit and deposited 20 feet to the east-northeast.  This direction of damage deposition was nearly opposite the direction of travel of the tornado. Numerous healthy small limbs of one half (0.5) inch diameter of healthy Australian pine were desposited toward the west-southeast across an unpaved dockfront access road. Video examinination determined some of the limbs were severed as the various roof covering structures struck the pine trees. It was at this point that the maximum wind estimate of 60 to 65 mph 3-second gust was demonstrated.||The tornado then entered the harbor waters at an oblique angle, causing a well-defined waterspout spray ring, and indicative of 3-second winds well in excess of 50 mph.  The now-waterspout crossed back over land as a tornado at the docks south of the 4th Avenue curve on Stock Island, where loose objects aboard vessels was lifted and deposited in a small turning basin. Eyewitnesses and video indicated the tornado no longer lifted debris or spray at that point, and seemingly dissipated.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: The eye of Hurricane Irma moved ashore in the Lower Florida Keys over Cudjoe Key at 9:10 am EDT Sunday, September 10, with a minimum central pressure of 929 mb and maximum sustained winds near 115 knots (130 mph).  The highest sustained winds in the Lower Florida Keys were measured at 61 knots (70 mph) at a NOAA National Ocean Service station at Key West Harbor, with a peak measured gusts at 120 mph at the Key Deer National Wildlife Refuge and a private residence on Big Pine Key.  Storm survey evidence of hurricane-force wind gusts include:  From Ohio, Missouri, Bahia Honda through Little Torch Keys, the strongest estimated winds were evident, possibly attributable to a mesoscale eyewall vortex circulation within the northeast quadrant of the eyewall.  A general path of of maximum wind damage occurred from the western end of Scout Key, just south of Big Pine Key Park, through Key Deer Boulevard north of South Street.  Complete roof structure failure involving snapped wood trusses was observed on several homes along with complete exterior wall failure on one waterfront home.  The path continued across Key Deer Boulevard where utility pole both of wood and hollow-spun concrete design were snapped with numerous spans lying in completely opposite directions.  The southern spans opposite to the direction of the mean wind.  Peak wind gusts were estimated 150 to 160 mph along the northern side of the apparent circulation.  Elsewhere across Big Pine Key, significant roofing loss and collapse of exterior walls on older mobile homes, large sections of roof coverings of all types, soffet damage and large metal roof, wall and door failures on modern metal building systems indicated more widespread estimated peak wind gusts of 120 to 130 mph.  From Ramrod Key through Sugarloaf Key, widespread business and residential roof covering damage of all types was observed, with isolated roof truss or gable end failures of older design.  It was noted a diagonal metal cross brace on an electric power transmission line across Niles Channel became detached from one vertical concrete column, indicative of significant deformation or flexing of the transmission towers.  Estimated peak wind gusts of 110 to 120 mph were attributed to this damage.  From Lower Sugarloaf Key through Big Coppitt Key, widespread small residential and business roof coverings with isolated structural gale end or overhang damage was noted especially in areas of open north wind exposure.  Isolated mobile home destruction including collapse of all walls was observed, although some modern mobile homes adjacent to properties with severe destruction exhibited few signs of cosmetic damage.  Estimated peak wind gusts 100 to 110 mph were attributed.  From Boca Chica Key through Key West, losses of roof coverings, soffet damage to residential homes and condominiums were noted, with two hotels exhibiting gable-end wood truss failures and sheathing of both mid-rise and two-story design.  Peak estimated wind gusts 90 to 100 mph were attributed, although the hotel mid-rise roof structure failure was in an area of open north wind exposure directly off the Gulf of Mexico may have indicated wind gusts in the 100 to 110 mph range.  Injuries estimated due to no operating hospitals nor rescue services available during the time of hurricane force wind impact.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Storm surge estimates of 5 to 8 feet were evident from Upper Sugarloaf Key through Bahia Honda, Ohio and Missouri Keys. Storm surge values of 3 to 5 feet were observed from Key West through Lower Sugarloaf Key.  Total water heights of 5 to 6 feet above ground level were observed along the east side of Big Pine Key, with wave wash marks up to 20 feet above mean high water along Long Beach Road on the oceanside.  Major damage to mobile homes and marinas was observed along the oceanside especially from Ramrod Key, through Big Pine Key, through Ohio Key.  The eastbound lanes of U.S. Highway One were washed out just east of the Bahia Honda State Park entrance.  Many residences and businesses were flooded at the maximum surge, ranging from 2 feet in the lee of the islands to up to 6 feet between 9:00 am and 1:00 pm EST November 10th.

events.cz_name: MONROE/MIDDLE KEYS
events.event_narrative: Hurricane-force wind damage from Marathon and Key Colony Beach revealed significant roof covering loss and isolated roof truss damage on older design oceanfront homes.  Older retail stores and a strip mall displayed complete uplift and collapse of wood box truss structures, while modern design structures displayed significant sections of roof covering loss, including metal panel-over-wood sheathing and built-up tar/rubber coverings.  Some older service station canopies displayed column buckling whereas modern designs displayed only slight racking or minor fascia damage.  Significant roof panel damage to mobile homes over both older and modern design.  All traffic signal masts remained in place, however signals were blown up to 90 degrees out of alignment.  Peak wind gusts of 100 to 115 mph were attributed.  From Grassy Key through the City of Layton and Long Key, several sections of wall panel loss on metal building systems, damage to built-up and shingle roof coverings, vinyl siding, and plastic paneled signs were noted.  Peak wind gusts estimated at 90 to 100 mph were attributed.  Injuries estimated due to lack of operating hospitals or rescue services during the hurricane impact.

events.cz_name: MONROE/MIDDLE KEYS
events.event_narrative: Storm surge estimates of 5 to 8 feet were evident from Marathon and Key Colony Beach, Grassy Key, and Duck Key. Storm surge values of 3 to 5 feet were observed from Conch Key through Long Key and Layton.  Total water height ranged from around 4 to 5 feet above ground level along the western edge of Marathon and Key Colony Beach to about 2 feet above ground level in Layton.  Numerous mobile homes were destroyed in Marathon as the storm tide pushed them off foundations toward U.S. Highway 1.

events.cz_name: MONROE/UPPER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Hurricane force wind damage was observed as follows:  Roof panels and vinyl siding were stripped from mobile homes, with vinyl siding damage on single family residences.  One service station canopy was completely overturned, without discernible deformities in the columns nor foundation.  Peak wind gusts were estimated at 90 to 100 mph.  In Tavernier, modern design large metal building systems exhibited failure of overhead doors on east and southeast-facing sides, with older designs including some pulled off exterior sheet panels.  Peak gusts near 100 mph were estimated.  From Key Largo through Ocean Reef, limited losses of built-up roof coverings and metal fascia from gas station canopies was observed.  Some older strip malls in Key Largo exhibited large losses of shingle and barrel tile coveraings.  Peak wind gusts near 90 mph were estimated.  Injuries are estimated due to no hospitals operating nor rescue services during the hurricane impact.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: Summary:  A waterspout or funnel cloud was observed backlit by |lightning over Florida Bay shortly before making landfall as a |tornado at Indian Mound Trail of the Indian Waterways subdivision of |Plantation Key, Islamorada. Large gumbo limbo tree limbs were downed |as well as the top of a palm tree, landing 20 yards from streetside |the front steps of a residence. And adjacent residence had a rolling |driveway gate completely dislodged from its mounts, pushed into a |trailered boat and car. The tornado continue to produce mostly |damage to large limbs of hardwood trees, including gumbo limbo and |mahogany, in a path rarely exceeded two residential properties in |width toward the east-northeast. An entire gutter and downspout |system was removed from a residence. Numerous loose items, including |filled trash cans and lawn/patio furniture was moved from the |backyards and understory of homes onto front lawns and streets. Most |of the observed damage in the Indian Waterways community were |consistent with 60 to 70 mph, with possible spot values near 75 mph.||The tornado crossed a patch of mangroves and undeveloped forest, and |reached greatest intensity at San Pedro Catholic Church. There, a |large tree split at the trunk, and an old-growth mahogany was |uprooted, falling toward the east onto a portion of the structure |connecting the rectory with the main church. Fortunately, the upper |portion of the tree did not substantially damage the roof, with no |leaks observed in the downpour that followed. However, several |barrel tiles were removed from the peak ridges forming the hip roof |pattern over the rectory, as well as from the southeast edge of the |church, onto the top of the church's main entrance. Numerous large |limbs were downed toward the east, with lightweight free-standing |signs deposited northward cross the tornado path from right to left.|Estimated wind speeds were maximized in the range of 90 to 100 mph |with maximum width near 60 yards. Good impact reference made to the |observed wind impacts at this location from recent Hurricane Irma, |all having previously been removed or repaired.  ||The tornado continued toward the east-northeast, crossing U.S. |Highway 1 and the Old Highway, but weakened such that only large |tree limbs were downed. From this point, the tornado likely moved |out over the oceanside as a waterspout into Hawk Channel, southwest |of the oceanside entrance to Tavernier Creek.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A second path, likely a continuation as the waterspout made landfall |near Lincoln Avenue on the far southwest portion of Tavernier's |oceanside. Progressive narrowing of the damage path down to nearly |30 yards as well as a turn toward the northwest or north-northwest |was observed.  Impacts lessened from near the waterfront, including |damaged fences and large limbs,gradually down to smaller limbs and |twigs was noted. No further impacts were observed northeast of Lowe |Street.  It is likely the wind speeds 55 to 65 mph were observed, |weakening to below 50 mph roughly 3 blocks from the waterfront.

events.cz_name: GULF OF MEXICO FROM WEST END OF SEVEN MILE BRIDGE TO HALFMOON SHOAL OUT TO 5 FATHOMS
events.event_narrative: A waterspout was observed to develop within Garrison Bight outside of the Palm Drive Bridge, and drifted slowly west, reaching a dock at a sailing center.  3 catamarans were considerably damaged due to overturning while tied to the dock, causing the dock planking to twist and detach from the pilings.  3 other vessels at the same dock had minor damage with ripped covers and canopy tops.  A video relayed by social media showed the width of the spray ring was only a few yards across, with the spray ring dissipating before the waterspout reached shore.  No damage was observed onshore at the sailing center nor an adjacent marina.

events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: A weak tornado, possibly a landfalling waterspout, produced EF0 damage along an intermittent path from Saguro Lane through Ocatillo Lane in the Flamingo Island subdivision of Marathon. The longest continuous damage path was approximately 100 yards long with a width of 25 yards. Damage was limited to live palm fronds and small broken branches, several found hanging in utility wires. Three homes were reported with minor roof damage, mainly to soffets blown upward into the roof cavity and a few shingles torn off. A second damage path, in-line with the path in Flamingo Island, was noted at the Marathon High School. One small tree was broken at the base, with an unsecured soccer goal overturned. A wooden canopy used as a sunscreen for the high school athletic field's press box was blown down.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Hurricane Laura, while still at tropical storm intensity, passed well south and southwest of the Florida Keys while tracking just off the south coast of Cuba, then turning northwest and crossing western Cuba west of Havana.  Sustained tropical storm force winds peaked at 34 knots (39 mph) at Key West International Airport, with a peak gust of 41 knots (47 mph).  Other notable peak wind gusts in the Lower Keys of Monroe County included a measured gust of 60 knots (69 mph) at the National Weather Service Office in Key West, 49 knots (56 mph) at the Keys Energy Service Building in downtown Key West, and 48 knots (55 mph) at the U.S. Coast Guard Sector in Key West.  Damage was limited to tree limbs and one downed medium-sized schefflera actinophylla (umbrella tree) in Key West.  Wind damage was estimated at about $2.5K.

events.event_narrative: Widespread tropical storm force winds in association with Hurricane Laura, which was passing along the south coast of Cuba and later turning northwest across western Cuba while at tropical storm intensity, occurred in the Straits of Florida offshore the Lower Florida Keys.  Peak sustained winds were measured at 45 knots (52 mph) with gusts to 50 knots (58 mph) at the new Sand Key Light C-MAN station.

Peak sustained winds were measured at 41 knots (47 mph) with gusts to 54 knots (62 mph) at an automated WeatherFlow station at Smith Shoal Light.

events.event_narrative: Spotters, automated Citizen Weather Observing Program gauges and law enforcement reported heavy rain and flooding of the bayside of the Overseas Highway on Lower Matecumbe and the Old Highway on Upper Matecumbe, including stalled vehicles. events.cz_name: MONROE
events.event_narrative: Key West Police Department reported numerous streets impassable due to flooding with stalled vehicles, including the Triangle (U.S. 1 and Roosevelt Boulevards), South Roosevelt and New Town neighborhoods along Northside Drive through Flagler Boulevard, and near Flagler and 5th Street.  Flooding later expanded to include the Bertha Street and Atlantic Boulevard neighborhoods, flooding a resident to a depth of 6 inches on Atlantic Drive.

events.cz_name: MONROE/UPPER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Sustained winds of 25 to 40 mph with frequent gusts of 40 to 60 mph were observed throughout the upper Florida Keys, with the strongest winds measured at a sustained speed of 41 mph at a private residential development in Rock Harbor with a peak gust of 58 mph. Wind gusts in excess of 50 mph were also measured at the Florida Keys Electric Cooperative Substation at Jewfish Creek, as well as at a residence on Plantation Key. Numerous trees and power lines were downed, with one house destroyed by a fallen tree in Key Largo along with one injury.  Approximately 1,000 customers were without power, mostly in Key Largo.  One wooden-post billboard was downed, with County Road 905, also known as Card Sound Road, blocked in several places due to downed trees between mile markers 3 and 8.

events.cz_name: MONROE/MIDDLE KEYS
events.event_narrative: Most tropical-storm force wind gusts were minimal, under 45 mph, and intermittent  due to rain squalls.  As the circulation center of Tropical Storm Eta passed through the middle Keys, a short period of sustained winds of 31 to 33 mph with gusts near 45 mph occurred in Marathon and Crawl Key.  The peak gust of 46 mph was measured at a meso-network station on Crawl Key.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Tropical Storm force wind gusts were mainly due to isolated rain squalls occurring well in advance to the northwest of the center of circulation. Peak winds were measured sustained at 49 mph with a gust to 56 mph at the USCG Sector Key West.  Isolated power outages to about 100 customers were reported.

events.cz_name: MONROE/UPPER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Storm Surge flooding of 1.5 to 2.0 feet above MHHW was noted oceanside of Key Largo, as well as the western side of Barnes Sound and Manatee Bay.  Oceanside neighborhoods were inundated by up to one foot, along with flooding impassible to vehicles in the parking lots of a resort along the north side of Jewfish Creek.  Minor overwash and a debris line was noted along Sea Oats Beach, an exposed oceanfront portion of U.S. Highway 1 in Lower Matecumbe Key.  Wave action estimated around 4 feet produced severe erosion on along the northbound right-of-way of U.S. Highway 1 south of Manatee Bay, destroying 3,000 feet of chain link fence as well as producing potholes and loss of protective riprap.

events.cz_name: MONROE/MIDDLE KEYS
events.event_narrative: A rise in water levels occurred within a few hours of the maximum northeast winds along the Bayside of Marathon, with water levels peaking about 2.3 feet above MHHW at Stirrup Key.  Water covered docks and inundated waterfront yards, however no significant flooding was observed in area streets.  Minor erosion occurred several hours prior at Key Colony Beach.

events.cz_name: HAWK CHANNEL FROM OCEAN REEF TO CRAIG KEY OUT TO THE REEF
events.event_narrative: Tropical Storm Eta produced a prolonged duration of tropical storm force winds along the Upper Keys reef tract, with peak sustained winds of 59 mph with gusts to 70 mph at Carysfort Reef Light, and sustained 45 mph with gusts to 58 mph at Alligator Reef Light.

events.cz_name: HAWK CHANNEL FROM WEST END OF SEVEN MILE BRIDGE TO HALFMOON SHOAL OUT TO THE REEF
events.event_narrative: Tropical Storm Eta passed to the east and north of the Lower Keys reef tract, producing only sporadic tropical storm force wind gusts at Sand Key.  Maximum sustained winds were measured at Sand Key Light at 45 mph with gusts to 49 mph.

events.event_narrative: Tropical Storm Eta passed north of the Gulf of Mexico waters north of the Lower Keys and beyond 5 fathoms, with peak sustained winds of 40 mph and gusts to 47 mph measured at Smith Shoal Light.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: As Tropical Storm Eta moved to the north northeast well to the west of the Lower Florida Keys, sustained winds of 25 to 30 mph with frequent gusts of 40 to 45 mph occurred.  Peak gusts of 44 mph were measured at Key West High School, and 43 mph at Cudjoe Key.  Minor power outages affecting less than 100 customers occurred in Key West.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Heavy wave action along South Roosevelt Boulevard and overwash resulted in closures of both South Roosevelt and Atlantic Boulevards in Key West.  However, no flat-water storm tide was noted by the Key West Harbor NOS tide gauge.

events.cz_name: MONROE/MIDDLE KEYS
events.event_narrative: Tropical storm wind gusts were measured up to 40 mph at the Florida Keys Marathon International Airport and unofficially up to 43 mph at a home weather station on Conch Key. Isolated tree limbs were downed with small power outages affecting fewer than 100 customers in the Marathon vicinity mainly between 0900 and 1300 EST on July 6th. No significant flooding or beach erosion was reported.

events.cz_name: MONROE/LOWER KEYS
events.event_narrative: Tropical storm force winds impacted the Lower Florida Keys of Monroe County, with peak sustained winds measured at 52 mph with gusts to 70 mph at Key West International Airport. Other notable wind measurements include sustained winds of 47 mph with gusts to 59 mph at the Naval Air Station Key West's Boca Chica Field, and a peak gust of 56 mph at the National Weather Service Forecast Office in Key West. Wind impacts included widely-separated instances of downed large tree limbs, mainly from Key West through the Saddlebunch Keys. A few power distribution circuits were out in the city of Key West due to fallen trees and tree limbs. Total customers impacted were estimated around 3500 in the Lower Keys.  Moderate beach erosion occurred on the oceanside of Key West.

events.cz_name: GULF OF MEXICO FROM EAST CAPE SABLE TO CHOKOLOSKEE 20 TO 60 NM OUT AND BEYOND 5 FATHOMS
events.event_narrative: Tropical storm marine winds occurred over the southeast Gulf waters beyond 5 fathoms offshore mainland Monroe County. An automated WeatherFlow station at Smith Shoal Light recorded peak winds sustained 48 knots with gusts to 58 knots at a height of 63 feet above mean sea level.

events.cz_name: HAWK CHANNEL FROM CRAIG KEY TO WEST END OF SEVEN MILE BRIDGE OUT TO THE REEF
events.event_narrative: Tropical storm force wind gusts briefly occurred over Hawk Channel west of Craig Key through the Seven Mile Bridge.  Peak winds measured at Sombrero Key Light were sustained at 28 knots with gusts to 38 knots.

events.cz_name: HAWK CHANNEL FROM WEST END OF SEVEN MILE BRIDGE TO HALFMOON SHOAL OUT TO THE REEF
events.event_narrative: Tropical storm force marine winds occurred over Hawk Channel west of Seven Mile Bridge through Halfmoon Shoal, with peak measurements at Sand Key Light sustained at 45 knots with gusts to 55 knots.

events.cz_name: STRAITS OF FLORIDA FROM WEST END OF SEVEN MILE BRIDGE TO SOUTH OF HALFMOON SHOAL OUT 20 NM
events.event_narrative: Per a U.S. Coast Guard media release, the U.S. Coast Guard suspended search for 9 souls missing at sea approximately 23 nautical miles southeast of Key West. A vessel with 22 souls on board departed Cuba and capsized approximately 1900 EST July 4th.  A good samaritan motor vessel and U.S. Coast Guard assets were able to rescue 13 survivors in the water.  Date of fatalities were assigned to the suspension of the search upon official presumption of lives lost at sea.
